formation.title: Unification of the Roof of the World
formation.text:
Tibet is united. From the windswept passes of the Changtang to the forested valleys of Kham, the plateau stands as one realm. But the question of how this realm shall be governed echoes through every monastery and fortress.

The Gelugpa monks offer a vision of sacred governance: the Ganden Phodrang, where the incarnate Dalai Lama guides both faith and statecraft through a council of learned ministers. In their monasteries, ten thousand monks study, pray, and prepare to administer an empire of the spirit.

Yet others look to the tradition of the Dharma Kings, those warrior-sovereigns who forged Tibet through conquest and patronage alike. A strong hand on the reins of power, they say, is what kept the plateau safe from the empires that ring its borders: China, Mongolia, the Mughals.

Which path shall Tibet follow?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Let the Dalai Lama's wisdom guide our nation

modifiers.name: Ganden Phodrang
modifiers.text: The unified theocratic government established under the Dalai Lama, merging spiritual authority with temporal power through the Kashag council. Monasteries serve as centers of learning, governance, and military coordination.

options.text: Tibet needs a warrior-king, not a monk

modifiers.name: Way of the Dharma Kings
modifiers.text: In the tradition of the great Tibetan kings (Songtsen Gampo, Trisong Detsen, and Ralpacan) a warrior-sovereign rules the plateau with firm authority, patronizing the dharma while commanding the armies that defend it.

advances.name: Warrior Monk Tradition
advances.text: The great monasteries of Tibet maintain their own armed contingents: the dob-dob, warrior monks who combine physical prowess with religious devotion, serving as enforcers and defenders of the monastic order.

advances.name: Yak Butter Economy
advances.text: The processing of yak butter for trade, ritual lamp offerings, and the iconic butter tea sustains both the monastic and pastoral economies of the plateau.

advances.name: Dzong Fortress System
advances.text: The dzong (a fortified monastery combining military garrison, administrative center, and religious complex) forms the backbone of Tibetan territorial control across the plateau.

advances.name: Tea-Horse Road
advances.text: The ancient caravan routes linking the tea-growing regions of China with the horse-breeding highlands of Tibet, facilitating the exchange of Tibetan horses, salt, and wool for Chinese tea, silk, and manufactured goods.

advances.name: Phagmodrupa Legacy
advances.text: The administrative traditions established during the Phagmodrupa dynasty, a balance of feudal authority and monastic oversight, continue to shape Tibetan governance.

advances.name: Sowa Rigpa
advances.text: The Science of Healing: Tibet's sophisticated medical system based on the Four Tantras, drawing from Indian, Chinese, Persian, and Bon traditions to treat ailments of body and mind.

event.title: The Four Tantras of Healing
event.text:
The tradition of Sowa Rigpa, the Science of Healing, reaches its full flowering. Building on the Gyushi, the Four Medical Tantras compiled in the twelfth century by Yuthok Yonten Gonpo, Tibetan physicians have developed one of the most sophisticated medical systems in Asia.

Drawing from Indian Ayurveda, Chinese medicine, Persian healing arts, and native Bon practices, the Four Tantras describe the human body as a landscape of elements in balance. Illness comes from their disturbance; healing comes from their restoration through herbs gathered at high altitude, mineral compounds, dietary regulation, and spiritual practice.

The establishment of medical colleges, Mentsekhang, in major monasteries ensures that this knowledge is preserved and transmitted. Physicians trained in these institutions serve communities across the plateau, their skills in demand from Nepal to Mongolia.

options.text: The Science of Healing illuminates our land

advances.name: Woodblock Printing Houses
advances.text: The great printing houses of Narthang, Derge, and Lhasa produce Buddhist scriptures from permanent woodblocks, spreading literacy and standardizing religious practice across the plateau.

event.title: Dharma in Ink and Wood
event.text:
The great printing houses of Tibet (at Narthang, Derge, and Lhasa) have transformed the preservation of Buddhist knowledge. Thousands of woodblocks, each painstakingly carved in reverse by master craftsmen, produce pages of scripture with a speed and accuracy that hand-copying could never match.

Unlike the movable type of China, Tibetan printers favored permanent woodblocks. A single block, once carved, could produce faithful copies for centuries: an appealing permanence for monasteries that saw themselves as guardians of an unbroken lineage of authentic Buddhist teaching. The Derge Parkhang alone houses over two hundred thousand blocks.

This revolution in textual production has spread literacy through the monastic system, standardized religious practice across the plateau, and created a body of printed literature rivaling any civilization on Earth.

options.text: The dharma spreads on printed wings

advances.name: Salt Lake Monopoly
advances.text: Tibet's vast salt lakes provide a monopoly on this essential commodity, traded south to Nepal and India in exchange for grain and manufactured goods.

advances.name: Sectarian Conflict
advances.text: The prolonged struggles between the Kagyu, Gelug, and Bon factions for supremacy have hardened Tibetan soldiers through generations of civil warfare.

advances.name: Mountain Pass Doctrine
advances.text: Centuries of defending the highest passes on Earth have produced a uniquely Tibetan approach to mountain warfare: using altitude, terrain, and the thin air itself as weapons against lowland invaders.

advances.name: Highland Textiles
advances.text: Tibetan wool and fur, gathered from yak herds and wild game at extreme altitudes, are prized commodities in the markets of India, China, and Central Asia.

advances.name: Khampa Cavalry Tradition
advances.text: The fierce horsemen of Kham, eastern Tibet's warrior culture, bring unmatched skill in mountain cavalry warfare, their horses bred for endurance at altitude.

event.title: The Warriors of Kham
event.text:
The people of Kham, the Khampas, are unlike any other Tibetans. Towering in stature, fierce in temperament, they are born to the saddle and the sword. Their reputation as warriors is unmatched on the plateau, and the mountain passes of eastern Tibet ring with the thunder of their horses.

For centuries, the Khampas have maintained a semi-autonomous existence, their tribal chiefs answering only loosely to Lhasa. Now, as Tibet's unified state matures, the question arises: how shall these formidable warriors be incorporated into the nation?

One path embraces their independence: granting the Khampa chieftains autonomy in exchange for their ferocious cavalry when called to war. The other demands integration, placing Khampa warriors under Lhasa's direct command, disciplining their fury into organized military power.

options.text: Let the Khampas ride free: their fury is our shield

modifiers.name: Khampa Rising
modifiers.text: The fierce Khampa horsemen of eastern Tibet have rallied to the banner, bringing their legendary martial prowess and intimate knowledge of mountain warfare to the national army.

options.text: Bring them under the Kashag's command

modifiers.name: Command of the Plateau
modifiers.text: The integration of the Khampa territories under centralized command has strengthened the state's grip on its vast eastern frontier, channeling the warriors' energy into disciplined service.

advances.name: Gelugpa Ascendancy
advances.text: The Yellow Hat school's rise to dominance transforms Tibetan religious life, establishing the Dalai Lama's spiritual authority across the plateau and into Mongolia.

advances.name: Dzong Garrison System
advances.text: Formalized military training for monks stationed at dzong fortresses, creating a professional garrison force that combines religious discipline with martial skill.

advances.name: Choyon Alliance
advances.text: The patron-priest relationship between Tibetan lamas and Mongol khans: a diplomatic masterwork where spiritual authority is exchanged for military protection and political legitimacy.

advances.name: Tibetan Coinage
advances.text: The development of a standardized Tibetan currency facilitates trade across the plateau and with neighboring powers, replacing the cumbersome barter of tea bricks and salt.

advances.name: Kashag Council
advances.text: The formal establishment of the Kashag, a council of ministers blending lay and clerical authority, as the primary administrative body of the Tibetan state.

advances.name: Potala Palace
advances.text: The construction of the Potala Palace on Marpo Ri: thirteen stories of stone, the greatest architectural achievement of the Tibetan plateau and the seat of both spiritual and temporal authority.

event.title: The Palace Above the Clouds
event.text:
The Potala Palace rises from the summit of Marpo Ri, the Red Hill of Lhasa. Thirteen stories of stone and timber, its White Palace houses the chambers of governance while the Red Palace contains chapels, tombs, and libraries of sacred texts. Tens of thousands of laborers and artisans have worked for decades to realize this vision.

Started in 1645 by the Fifth Dalai Lama, the palace took nearly fifty years to complete: its construction continuing in secret after his death under the stewardship of the regent Desi Sangye Gyatso. With over a thousand rooms, ten thousand shrines, and two hundred thousand statues, it stands as the greatest architectural achievement of the Tibetan plateau.

The Potala is more than a palace. It is a statement: that Tibet's civilization, nestled among the highest mountains on Earth, can produce works to rival any empire below.

options.text: A monument worthy of the Roof of the World

modifiers.name: Glory of the Potala
modifiers.text: The magnificent Potala Palace crowns Marpo Ri hill above Lhasa, its white and red towers visible for miles across the valley. A monument to the unity of spiritual and temporal power, it inspires awe in all who behold it.

advances.name: Regency Tradition
advances.text: The pragmatic administrative tradition established by Desi Sangye Gyatso, who governed Tibet during the interregnum after the Fifth Dalai Lama's death, concealing it for fifteen years while consolidating state power.

advances.name: Narthang Printing Expansion
advances.text: The expansion of woodblock printing from Narthang and Derge to dozens of monasteries across the plateau, creating a network of scholarly production unmatched in Central Asia.

advances.name: Plateau Cavalry Tactics
advances.text: The refinement of cavalry tactics for the unique demands of high-altitude warfare: lighter equipment, horses bred for thin air, and an emphasis on rapid movement across vast distances.

advances.name: Silk and Musk Trade
advances.text: Tibet's position astride the routes between China and South Asia enables a lucrative trade in luxury goods: musk, silk, medicinal herbs, and precious metals flow through highland passes.

advances.name: Monastic Taxation
advances.text: The systematization of monastic estates and their taxation provides the Ganden Phodrang government with a reliable revenue base, as monasteries serve simultaneously as landlords, educational institutions, and tax collectors.

advances.name: Plateau Modernization
advances.text: Attempts to modernize Tibetan institutions: introducing new administrative methods, expanded education, and engagement with the wider world while preserving the plateau's unique cultural identity.

advances.name: Tibetan Standing Army
advances.text: The creation of Tibet's first professional standing army, replacing the reliance on monastic levies and tribal cavalry with trained, disciplined soldiers equipped with modern arms.

advances.name: Communal Land Traditions
advances.text: Tibet's communal land management practices and polyandrous family structures, which stabilize population and ensure sustainable use of the plateau's limited agricultural resources.

advances.name: Dharma Preservation
advances.text: The systematic effort to preserve and expand Tibetan Buddhist scholarship: copying texts, training scholars, and maintaining the monastic universities that have served as repositories of knowledge for centuries.

advances.name: Plateau Trade Network
advances.text: The maturation of Tibet's highland trade system: connecting Lhasa to Calcutta, Kathmandu, Beijing, and the Silk Road through a network of caravans, trading posts, and established commercial relationships.

destiny.name: Destiny of Tibet
destiny.text: The plateau has been unified before, and twice by opposite means. The Yarlung tsenpo did it with cavalry and treaty, holding the Hexi corridor and taking tribute from Chang'an. The Gelug hierarchs did it with monasteries and magistrates, governing from Lhasa without a king at all. Both are still available. The choice is which Tibet the world will have to deal with.

event.title: The Question of the Plateau
event.text: The ministers put it plainly. Tibet can be governed as a church or as a kingdom, and the two need different men in the same offices. The abbots want the dzong staffed with monks and the revenue pledged to the great houses of prayer. The lords of Kham and Ngari want a tsenpo, a muster, and the old frontier back. Delay favours neither.

options.text: The plateau will choose its own road

destiny.name: The Lhasa Settlement
destiny.text: In 1642 the Fifth Dalai Lama was installed as sovereign of Tibet and the Gelug order became the state itself. The seat of government is moved from Sakya to Lhasa, Shigatse grows around the monastery of Tashilhunpo, and the seats of the two great hierarchs are brought under one administration. The sectarian wars that consumed the plateau for three centuries are settled by making one sect the government.

conditions.text: Shigatse is ours and has been built up to a development of at least 14

event.title: One Sect, One State
event.text: The Gelug hierarchs of Lhasa and the abbots of Shigatse have agreed terms, and the agreement is that there are no terms: the yellow hats govern. Three centuries of sectarian war end not in compromise but in a settlement, and the monasteries that resisted find their estates transferred to those that did not. The plateau is quiet for the first time in living memory.

destiny.name: The Dzong Magistracy
destiny.text: Fifty-three fortress-districts carry Ganden Phodrang authority to the edges of the plateau. Each dzong holds the granary, the corvee register, the militia muster and the court, and each is run by a paired appointment (one lay magistrate, one monk) rotated every three years so no magistrate strikes local roots. Gyantse, whose fortress has stood since 1390, is built up as the model of them, and Chamdo on the Kham road is held directly.

conditions.text: Gyantse is ours and has been built up to a development of at least 9

event.title: The Fortresses of the Realm
event.text: The dzong are ready: granary, register, muster and court under one roof, from Gyantse in Tsang to Chamdo on the Kham road. What remains is deciding who sits in them. The Yiktsang has monks enough to fill every post; the Tse-yik's noble registry has men who already know the districts and the families in them.

options.text: Paired appointments, monk and layman, rotated every three years

modifiers.name: Dzong Network
modifiers.text: Paired lay and monastic magistrates rotate through fifty-three fortress-districts on three-year terms. No magistrate strikes local roots, every district keeps its granary and muster in working order, and the corvee turns out when it is called.

options.text: Staff them from the noble registry: they know the ground

modifiers.name: Lay Magistracy
modifiers.text: The dzong are staffed from the Tse-yik's noble registry. The great houses get the offices, the offices get men who already know the districts, and the trade that moves through the fortress towns is taxed by people with an interest in it continuing. The houses do not give the offices back.

destiny.name: The Great Prayer Festival
destiny.text: For twenty-one days each year the lay administration of Lhasa suspends itself and a Drepung abbot governs the city with the power to fine, flog and banish. Twenty thousand monks fill the Jokhang precinct. Tsongkhapa founded it in 1409 as a festival; the Ganden Phodrang keeps it as the annual proof that dharma and state are the same thing. The festival needs a city fit to hold it, and Derge in Kham under the direct hand of Lhasa.

conditions.text: Lhasa is ours and has been built up to a development of at least 30

event.title: Twenty Thousand Monks
event.text: The Monlam Chenmo has outgrown the Jokhang precinct. A permanent pavilion would hold the whole assembly and make the festival's authority over Lhasa a matter of architecture rather than custom. There is another view: that the sectarian question was never truly settled and the moment to settle it by decree is now, while the yellow hats hold every office worth holding.

options.text: Build the pavilion: let the festival speak for the state

modifiers.name: The Great Prayer
modifiers.text: A permanent pavilion holds the whole Monlam assembly. For three weeks each year the festival magistrate governs Lhasa outright, and the unity of dharma and state is staged in front of the entire population rather than argued in council.

options.text: Settle the sects by decree while the offices are ours

modifiers.name: Gelug Primacy
modifiers.text: The sectarian question is closed by decree while the yellow hats hold every office worth holding. Rival estates are transferred, rival lineages are recognised as branches, and the plateau's religious map is redrawn to match its administrative one. The other schools are no longer suffered as rivals.

destiny.name: The Tsenpo Restored
destiny.text: Tibet had kings before it had abbots. The Yarlung dynasty came out of the valley of Nedong with a sworn aristocracy and a cavalry army, and the monasteries served the crown rather than replacing it. Restoring that crown means the old seat at Nedong is rebuilt as a town, no emperor in China is acknowledged as overlord, and the plateau's warlike clans as far as Dartsedo answer to a throne again.

conditions.text: Chose Way of the Dharma Kings
Nedong is ours and has grown into a town

event.title: A Crown Out of Storage
event.text: The regalia of the Yarlung kings has been kept in a monastery storeroom for six hundred years, catalogued as a relic. It is brought out, and the clans of Kham who would never bow to an abbot come to Lhasa to swear. The abbots are told the crown protects the dharma. Everyone present understands the order of precedence has changed.

destiny.name: The Plateau Marches
destiny.text: The Himalayan passes are the empire's gates: Ladakh to the west, the Nepalese valleys to the south. The old empire held them with permanent garrisons and treated the mountains as a frontier to be administered rather than a wall to hide behind.

event.title: The Gates of the Mountains
event.text: Ladakh and the Nepalese valleys are taken, and the passes with them. Holding a frontier this long is a question of method: permanent garrisons in stone, fed and paid from Lhasa, or the Kham horse-clans riding it as they have always ridden it, cheaper and faster and answerable to their own chiefs.

modifiers.name: The Marchlands
modifiers.text: Stone garrisons on the Himalayan passes, fed and paid from Lhasa. The frontier is administered rather than merely watched, and an army operating along it is never far from a supplied post.

options.text: Raise the Kham clans and let them ride the frontier

modifiers.name: Khampa Levies
modifiers.text: The Kham horse-clans ride the frontier as they always have, answerable to their own chiefs and mustered by summons rather than by pay. Cheaper than garrisons and faster than garrisons, and the chiefs who lead them keep their own counsel.

destiny.name: Bod Chen Po
destiny.text: Great Tibet, as the Tang chancery called it. Between 786 and 848 the tsenpo held the Hexi corridor outright, cutting China off from Central Asia and taxing the whole silk trade at Shazhou and Ganzhou. In 763 a Tibetan army took Chang'an and installed its own emperor. That empire is the one being rebuilt.

event.title: Great Tibet
event.text: Shazhou and Ganzhou are ours, and with them the corridor that carries every caravan between China and the west. The Tang chancery called this state Bod chen po and negotiated with it as an equal. The corridor can be held as the old empire held it, in force, with the garrisons and the horse-herds that implies, or it can simply be taxed, which costs less and offends fewer.

options.text: Hold it as the tsenpo held it

modifiers.name: Bod Chen Po
modifiers.text: The Hexi corridor is held in force, as the tsenpo held it: garrisons at Shazhou and Ganzhou, remount herds behind them, and the memory of every siege the plateau's armies have ever conducted written into the way they conduct the next one.

options.text: Take the tolls and leave the caravans their peace

modifiers.name: The Corridor Tolls
modifiers.text: The caravans are taxed rather than commanded. Shazhou and Ganzhou keep their merchants, their merchants keep their routes, and the plateau takes a share of everything that moves between China and the west without paying for the garrisons that holding it outright would need.

units.name: Dob-dob
units.text: Warrior monks from Tibet's great monasteries, the dob-dob are fearsome combatants who combine religious fervor with physical prowess. Armed with staves and slings, they patrol monastic grounds and form shock infantry in times of war.

units.name: Khampa Horsemen
units.text: The mounted warriors of Kham are born to the saddle. Armed with swords, bows, and matchlocks, these fierce cavalrymen are expert raiders who know every mountain pass and valley of eastern Tibet.

units.name: Garrison Monks
units.text: Disciplined monk-soldiers trained to defend the dzong fortress-monasteries. Combining religious conviction with military drill, they form the permanent garrison force of the Tibetan state.

units.name: Plateau Riders
units.text: Elite high-altitude cavalry equipped with lighter arms and riding horses bred for the thin air of the plateau. Fast and agile, they excel at flanking maneuvers across the vast Tibetan steppe.

units.name: Tibetan Regulars
units.text: Professional soldiers of Tibet's first standing army, trained in modern military discipline while retaining the mountain warfare expertise that has always been the plateau's greatest defense.

buildings.name: Dzong
buildings.text: A massive fortress-monastery that serves as military stronghold, administrative center, and religious complex. Built on commanding heights with thick stone walls, the dzong is the backbone of Tibetan territorial control.

buildings.name: Tea-Horse Trading Post
buildings.text: A caravan station on the ancient Tea-Horse Road, where Tibetan horses, salt, and wool are exchanged for Chinese tea, silk, and manufactured goods. These posts sustain the commercial lifeline of the plateau.

buildings.name: Mentsekhang
buildings.text: A medical college teaching Sowa Rigpa: the Tibetan Science of Healing. Physicians trained here master the Four Tantras, treating ailments through herbal remedies, mineral compounds, and spiritual practice.

buildings.name: Printing House
buildings.text: A monastic woodblock printing workshop where master craftsmen carve scripture into permanent blocks. A single printing house may hold tens of thousands of blocks, producing Buddhist texts for distribution across the plateau.

buildings.name: Butter Lamp Workshop
buildings.text: A facility for processing yak butter into the ritual lamps that illuminate every monastery on the plateau, as well as the butter tea that sustains both monks and nomads in the thin, cold air.

where.text: The location's raw material is Livestock

buildings.name: Salt Warehouse
buildings.text: A storage and processing facility for the salt harvested from Tibet's high-altitude salt lakes, one of the plateau's most valuable trade commodities.

where.text: The location's raw material is Salt

buildings.name: Choyon Temple
buildings.text: A grand temple complex dedicated to the patron-priest relationship that binds Tibet to its Mongol allies, serving as a center of diplomatic ceremony and cultural exchange.

buildings.name: Highland Wool Workshop
buildings.text: A textile workshop processing the fine wool of Tibetan yaks and sheep into cloth prized across Asia for its warmth and durability.

buildings.name: Potala Shrine
buildings.text: A sacred devotional complex inspired by the architectural grandeur of the Potala Palace, serving as a center of Buddhist worship, artistic patronage, and cultural prestige.

buildings.name: Communal Granary
buildings.text: A community food storage facility following Tibet's ancient tradition of communal resource management, ensuring survival through the harsh winters of the highest plateau on Earth.

buildings.name: Monlam Pavilion
buildings.text: A permanent hall for the Great Prayer Festival, raised beside the Jokhang so the twenty thousand monks who come each spring no longer have to fill the streets. Outside the festival weeks it houses the debating courtyards and the almonry, and the abbots who run both are the same men who run the city for three weeks a year.

buildings.name: Tsenpo Citadel
buildings.text: The war-capital of the Yarlung kings rebuilt in stone: muster ground, armoury, remount pens and the royal guard's barracks inside one wall. The old empire ran its campaigns from places like this, and an army that assembles here is fed and horsed before it reaches the frontier.

list.name: Kashag Council
list.text: Codified by Qianlong's 1751 reforms after the murder of the lay regent Gyurme Namgyal, the Kashag seated four kalon ministers in a single chamber: three lay nobles drawn from the great Lhasa houses (Lhalu, Yuthok, Phunkhang) and one monk-kalon nominated by the Dalai Lama. No minister could act without the others' consent. The Kashag was the empire of paperwork that moved the plateau's daily business and proved the most stable institution Tibet built, but it embedded the lay aristocracy permanently inside the Ganden Phodrang.

list.name: Yiktsang Ecclesiastical Secretariat
list.text: The parallel cabinet of the four trungyikchenmo, the chief monk-secretaries who handled every matter touching the monasteries: ordinations, doctrinal disputes, monastic estates, the audit of the Dalai Lama's labrang, and the appointment of dzongpon to monastic dzongs. Mirroring the Kashag in every prefecture, the Yiktsang made the Ganden Phodrang a literal dual administration, and made the clergy structurally indispensable to every act of state.

list.name: Densa Sum: The Three Pillars
list.text: The three great Gelugpa monasteries of the Lhasa plain: Sera (founded 1419 by Sakya Yeshe), Drepung (1416 by Jamyang Choje, the largest monastery in the world at over ten thousand monks), and Ganden (1409 by Tsongkhapa, seat of the Ganden Tripa). Their abbots could veto regency appointments and their representatives sat on the Tsongdu national assembly. During the 1862 Wangchuk Shatra coup it was Drepung monks who marched on the Potala. The Three Pillars made Tibetan Buddhism a state-political force, not just a faith.

list.name: Mi-tser Estate System
list.text: The plateau's revenue-estates were allotted in three categories: shung-gyu (government estates worked by tsongpa subjects), choji (monastic estates supporting specific tulku), and gerba (hereditary noble estates of the great Lhasa houses). Every estate carried obligations of u-lag (forced transport corvee), tsa-tang (army provisions), and produce-render. The mi-tser (literally 'human-property') owed labour to whichever estate-holder controlled their natal village. The system kept the nobility solvent and the army supplied, but bound the peasantry to their birthplace by inheritable obligation.

list.name: Dzongpon Magistracy
list.text: The district magistrates of the fifty-three dzong-fortresses that anchored Ganden Phodrang authority across the plateau, from Shigatse and Gyantse in Tsang to Chamdo and Markham in Kham. Each dzong was administered by a paired appointment: one lay dzongpon drawn from the Tse-yik's noble registry, one monk-dzongpon from the Yiktsang's roll, both rotated on three-year terms so that no magistrate could strike permanent local roots. The dzong housed the granary, the corvee register, the militia muster, and the local court.

list.name: Monlam Chenmo Great Prayer Festival
list.text: Founded by Tsongkhapa in 1409, the Great Prayer Festival was made the central ritual of the Ganden Phodrang state. For twenty-one days from the fourth day of the first lunar month, the city's lay administration suspended itself and the Drepung Shartse abbot took on the office of tsogchen shal-ngo, festival magistrate, with police authority over Lhasa and the right to fine, flog, or banish any inhabitant. Twenty thousand monks crowded the Jokhang precinct to recite, debate, and process behind the great Maitreya image. The festival staged the unity of dharma and state to the entire population each year.
